title: ICDiffAD: Time Series Anomaly Detection via Controlled Diffusion
one_liner: A diffusion model that detects abnormalities in time series data by learning to reconstruct normal patterns while carefully controlling the randomness at each step.
lead: Time series anomaly detection faces a core problem: diffusion models (a type of generative model that learns by gradually adding and removing noise) excel at capturing normal patterns, but their randomness makes them unreliable for detecting what is abnormal. ICDiffAD fixes this by using two techniques: a scheduler that controls noise levels during learning, and a way to initialize generation from the input itself, balancing the model's flexibility with the accuracy needed for detection.

problem.h2: Why diffusion models struggle with time series anomalies
paras: A diffusion model learns by watching data get progressively corrupted by noise, then learning to reverse the process—to clean the noise away step by step. For time series (sequences like stock prices or sensor readings over time), this works well at capturing what normal looks like. But here is the catch: randomness is baked into every step. Even when reconstructing the same input twice, the model gives slightly different outputs because it is sampling from a probability distribution at each step. For detecting anomalies, this variance is fatal—you can't reliably say whether something is abnormal if you get different reconstructions every time.

A naive approach would be to just accept this variance and hope the reconstruction error for true anomalies is always higher than the noise. It fails because the randomness in the reconstruction overshadows the signal you are trying to detect. Your detector becomes unreliable.

callout.html: ICDiffAD uses two controls to tame randomness: a scheduler that manages noise intensity during learning, and a way to seed the generation from the input itself.

paras: The paper changes two things. First, it introduces an SNR Scheduler—a schedule that controls the signal-to-noise ratio (a measure of how loud the signal is compared to noise) at each step of learning. Second, it uses an SNR Implicit Conditioning Mechanism, which means starting the reverse process from the input itself, partially corrupted, rather than from pure random noise. Together, these make reconstructions much less random while still capturing complex patterns.

hidden.name: Signal-to-noise ratio at each step
paras: Signal-to-noise ratio, or SNR, is a number that measures how loud the true data is compared to the noise layered on top. A high SNR means the signal is clear; a low SNR means noise dominates. The paper's key insight is that controlling SNR directly during training tells the model exactly how much noise to expect at each stage, making learning predictable.

Traditional diffusion models use a fixed noise schedule (more noise at the start, less at the end), but ICDiffAD learns which SNR values work best at each step. When reconstructing for anomaly detection, the scheduler ensures that initializing from a partially corrupted input is consistent with how the model was trained—the model expects that level of corruption and handles it cleanly.

heat.caption: Darker shows higher signal-to-noise ratio. Training learns to handle each level. Test uses the same SNR progression to initialize fairly.

reads.html: SNR is just how clear the signal is versus how much noise is added. The scheduler picks the right clarity level at each step.

The SNR Scheduler governs training through quantifiable noise scales, enabling the model to learn normative patterns reliably. For inference (when the finished model answers on new data), the SNR Implicit Conditioning Mechanism initializes reverse diffusion from partially corrupted inputs aligned with the learned SNR progression.

mechanism.h2: Why controlling noise makes anomaly detection work
paras: The core insight: diffusion models work by gradually peeling away noise, like a sculptor refining details. But this process comes at a cost—randomness. Every sample draws from a probability distribution (the pattern of how often each output occurs), so identical inputs produce slightly different outputs. For anomaly detection, this noise in the reconstruction is a catastrophe because you can't tell if high error means the input is abnormal or just that the randomness happened to mess up that sample.

ICDiffAD solves this in two parts. First, the SNR Scheduler makes training deterministic by controlling noise intensity precisely. The model learns: at this SNR level, here is what normal data looks like. Second, initializing from the input itself (corrupted to match the scheduled SNR) anchors the reconstruction to the input. The model does not have to imagine new data from scratch; it just learns what the input would look like if you removed the noise. Anomalous parts of the input cannot be cleaned up because the model has never seen that pattern in normal training data, so they remain garbled. Normal parts get cleaned crisply. The gap is now reliable because both normal and anomalous reconstructions are reproducible.

Why does this work mechanically? Diffusion models learn from data by computing gradients—directions to adjust the numbers inside the model to match observed patterns. When you control SNR, you teach the model the expected noise level at each step. When you initialize from the partially corrupted input, you are saying: assume this input is mostly normal with added noise; clean it up. The model either succeeds (it removes noise from normal patterns) or fails (anomalies stay corrupted). Because this process is not random—it follows a fixed path through learned rules—the result is reproducible and reliable.

items.html: If the test SNR schedule does not match training, the model encounters noise levels it did not learn. The reconstruction becomes unreliable and anomalies are missed.

items.b: Initialization from pure noise instead of corrupted input.
items.html: Reverting to standard diffusion (starting from random noise) reintroduces the original variance problem. The paper's benefit disappears.
If the training data is skewed (many samples of one anomaly type but not others), the model learns to expect those patterns. Other anomaly types may not be flagged.

The SNR scheduler is fixed consistently across training and testing; initialization always uses the corrupted input; training data covers a wide range of normal behavior. Under these conditions, anomalies stand out clearly and reproducibly.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple time series with known normal regions and planted anomalies (e.g., a sine wave with occasional spikes). Train ICDiffAD on only the normal regions using the SNR scheduler. Then run inference on new data, comparing ICDiffAD to naive diffusion. Reconstruct the same anomalous sample three times. With ICDiffAD, the reconstruction should be nearly identical each time and flag the spike reliably. With naive diffusion, the three reconstructions should differ noticeably and detection should be inconsistent (sometimes catching the spike, sometimes missing it).
demo.metric_eq: F1 score = (2 * precision * recall) / (precision + recall); precision = correct detections / all detections; recall = correct detections / all real anomalies
demo.closing: The demo must make it unmissable that controlled noise gives reproducible detections while naive diffusion gives noisy, inconsistent results.
